utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones I represent Mr. Naser Oric. We're joined by our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour, which is in the absence of the witness we wanted to put on the record that in terms of P575, an exhibit that was used yesterday and a document which may be used today which is 02116778 to 02116783, we challenge the authenticity of those documents. According to receipt 32 of disclosure it's Serb-sources material and we would want more details of the chain of custody and we may request to inspect the originals. But I just wanted to state that now for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime -- but on this -- I'll raise this at some other point in another time so as not to take time off today's sitting. Any further preliminaries? I see none. All right. We can proceed. In the meantime while she is escorting, we handed down the Rule 92 bis, as you know, decision yesterday. We received the Prosecution response regarding protective measures motion and we also received the translation for -- of document C5. Right. I have also arranged for an appointment with a member of the registrar to have a written statement as to what procedure they have adopted in the past when documents were -- left this Tribunal for examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand it was done in at least three occasions, so -- and then I will come back to you when I have that available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I wonder if in light of that, Your Honour, we indicated yesterday that we would submit our motion today. It might be prudent to wait to see what the registry's practice is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, Madam Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you please stand up. On behalf of the Tribunal I would like to welcome you to this Tribunal, to this courtroom. You are going to be a witness for the Prosecution in this case instituted against Naser Oric as a Defence witness in this case instituted against Naser Oric. My name is Carmel Agius and I come from the Mediterranean island of Malta. I am flanked on my right by Judge Hendrik Brydensholt of the Kingdom of Denmark, and to my left I have Judge Professor Albin Eser from Germany. We are presiding over this trial. Since you are here to give evidence our Rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration which is contained in a piece of paper that is going to be given to you now. This is solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, an undertaking, a solemn undertaking, that in the course of your truth you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please take the text in your hand, read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Please make yourself comfortable. Today the two parties, Defence and Prosecution, together with us, we will be making a big effort to try and finish with your testimony today, and that would enable you to go back home as early as possible. We need your help, too, because otherwise you will be here at least until Monday. And your help will consist in trying to answer all questions as brief -- as briefly as possible, as precisely, as truthfully, but also as concisely, as briefly as possible. Don't try to give more information than you are asked for. And if there are questions that you can answer with a mere yes or no, then please do so. And if you need to explain any further, ask our permission to explain further and I will give you permission. The first series of questions will come, of course, from the Defence side, since you are a Defence witness. It's Mr. Jones who will be examining you in chief. He will then be followed by Mr. Wubben up on cross-examination. Your responsibility is to answer all questions, irrespective of who is putting the questions to you, in a truthful manner and to the best of my ability. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And good morning, Ms. Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Please give the Court your full name, first of all.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Suhra Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And please tell me if the following details are correct. First, that you were born on the 24th of February, 1965, in Potcaus in Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You enter a primary school and high school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before the war broke out you traded drinks for the company Prokuplje and you worked from your home?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your husband's name was Muriz Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You have two children, a boy born on the 1st of December, 1986, Munir?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And a daughter who was born on the 25th of January, 1990, called Emina?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you work as a secretary for Women of Podrinje, an association called Women of Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what that association is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It is an association taking care of the affairs with regard to missing persons in the Bratunac area between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you lose any family members in that period, 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I lost 23 members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, at the start of the war were you living in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before the war, was Bjelovac Muslim, Serb, or mixed?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How many Muslims were there in Bjelovac in 1992? And I'm not talking just about the centre, I'm talking --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: About 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that 200 people or 200 houses?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: 200 people. And there were 40 Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before the war among the inhabitants of Bjelovac, did you divide the village into a Serb Bjelovac and a non-Serb Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how many Muslim houses were there in the centre of Bjelovac? You've told us that there were 40 in the area, but how much in the real centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: In the centre of Bjelovac there were 11 Muslim houses and six Muslim holiday homes, secondary residences.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your house, was that only in a Muslim section of town or did you have Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: My house was in a mixed section of town because Bjelovac was a mixed town. My next-door neighbour was Rado Milovanovic, and on the other side my next-door neighbour was Rade Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, please answer with a yes or no whether the following people has houses in Bjelovac. First of all Hajrudin Begzadic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sead Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Izet Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Juso Efendic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Rifet Dautbasic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were there other Muslim houses besides those that I've mentioned in the centre of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the house of Muriz Sinanovic, Rahmana Sinanovic, the Alica's house, and the Efendic family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And these people, they were all known, were they, to the Serb inhabitants of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know the houses of the people with the surname Mujic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were those houses in Bjelovac, not the centre, strictly speaking, but in the Bjelovac village?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were those people Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know the houses of the people with the surname Jahic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, were their houses in Bjelovac and were they Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Their houses were in Bjelovac and they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, do you know the people with the surname Lolic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the same question: Were the houses in Bjelovac and were they Serb or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Their houses were in Bjelovac and they're Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, among the inhabitants of Bjelovac, Serbs and Muslims, was it ever considered or said that those houses I've just mentioned of Mujic, Jahic, and Lolic, were outside of Bjelovac, for example in Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were always in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know an area called Jovanovici?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is Jovanovici a hamlet of its own separate from Bjelovac and Sikiric, or is it part of either of those villages?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: That's kind of separate because it was a family name, so that's why it was called Jovanovici and it's between Bjelovac and another locality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But the interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What's the other locality, apart from Bjelovac, that you mentioned, where Jovanovici is situated?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Those six Jovanovics' houses, they were called -- the hamlet was called Jovanovici because there were several houses belonging to the people called Jovanovic and that's why it was called like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What's on the other side of Jovanovici if you're going towards Skelani?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Sikiric, in the direction of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I think that clarifies it. Do you know Slavka Matic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is he illiterate to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: She is not illiterate. She can read and write because she used to come to my house. We would watch films and read newspapers and magazines together. So as far as I know she is not illiterate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why would watching films show you that she's not illiterate?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Because we were sitting together and she could read things in the screen and also we used to read the papers or magazines and we would clarify and explain things to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "reading things on the screen," are you talking about subtitles or are you talking about titles on the screen? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever appeared written on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Where was her house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Her house was 300 metres away from my mine in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So it was not in Jovanovici?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And earlier I asked you about Hajrudin Begzadic. Can you tell us whether he had any health problems before the war?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, what did he have?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: He had head surgery before the war and he had pains in his right leg and he couldn't move about very easily. And he didn't do his military service because he had problems with his leg, first of all, so he was deemed unfit. And then later on he had surgery on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And those problems you've described, did he have them, to your knowledge, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Both in 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned one of your neighbours was Rade Ilic. In early 1992 did you ever notice any unusual incidents around his house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was putting clothes out to dry when a car drove by and a teacher called Sarac, I can't remember the rest of his name, came. He used to teach in Bjelovac, and he came with Rade's relative and he called Rade. He was not there, but his wife came out, she was called Rosa Ilic and they were taking rifles and uniforms, camouflage uniforms, out of the car. It was all new and wrapped in cellophane. And they were getting the ammunition out of the car as well. And he said, Okay, Roso, this is for Rado to see that his cousin has arms, too, and not only himself. And they took everything into Rado's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us when this was in terms of the month?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you mentioned rifles and uniforms, camouflage uniforms. Was there anything else which was taken out of the car?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Rifles, uniform, and ammunition, and white belts. Those military belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is this something you saw with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I myself saw all that because it was about 5 metres away, because there is just a fence between our two properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And around this time, April 1992, were there any -- any incidents which made you feel insecure?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At some point every evening at around 10.00 when it was already dark, we could hear screams and shots being fired from the banks of the river Drina. And they would take people to the banks of the river, the beaches along the river, and they would be taken to the river and they would be shot, and the bodies would be thrown into the river to be washed away. It was terrible. We were all in fear and expecting a knock on the door at any minute and expecting to be dragged down to the river as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this area, Ledine. Where is that in relation to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It is just below the houses in Bjelovac, between the houses and the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know of any people who disappeared in this way, the names of any people?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do know two who perished at Ledine. Kadrija who used to be a police officer, or rather -- no, Kadrija and Fehim, and Fehim was the police officer, and Kadrija's wife walked past my house and she was crying and she was saying that Kadrija had been taken in the direction of Drina from their house in Bratunac [as interpreted] and she was looking for the body in order to be able to organise a burial. And the man's name was Kadrija Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for the record, Fehim, the police officer, do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, Kurtovic, Fehim Kurtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, at this time were there any incidents on the road which made you fear for your safety?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It went on this terrible fear for a number of days. It was terribly scary to be in the streets of Bjelovac. There were three Golf cars, a red one, a white one, and a yellow one, and in every car there was a uniformed girl and there was a rifle sticking out of the window and the muffler would have been taken off. So it made so much noise, I mean the cars, and it was so scary and we hardly dared get into our own backyards. And it went on for a number of days and they would drive around three or four times a day, and there was a girl, a uniformed girl, in every car.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were these, to your knowledge, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as we knew, they were Serbs, but Serbs had uniforms and arms; we didn't have anything and we didn't know anything about it. Because those Golf cars had been stolen from the Muslims in Bratunac, all three cars. I forgot the name of the rightful owners, but all of the cars had been taken away from the Muslims in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you actually knew the rightful owners of those cars, even if you can't remember the names now?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I did know, but this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you actually no longer felt comfortable sleeping in your house at night?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were all living in fear. We didn't dare go out. And one night when we went to bed at around 10.00 in the evening, Slavoljub Filipovic and my next-door neighbour called Rade Ilic called my husband, Muriz Sinanovic, and the windows were open so I got up as well. I could see them standing there in camouflage uniforms carrying rifles and they asked where Muriz was, and I said that he had gone to bed. And they said that he should come out and not switch the lights on, and that's what I told him to do. And he went out of the house. He was standing at the stairs in his pyjamas in the dark and they talked for a long time and I was getting ever more nervous and I feared that they would take him away and because of this nervousness and because of my fear, I just had to go in the direction of the door and I could here Slavoljub Filipovic trying to convince, in a rather forceful way, trying to convince my husband. And he was telling him that he wanted his lorry and Muriz said he wouldn't do that and he said that it would be given to TO Fakovici or Skelani. And he said it would be much for you to give the lorry to us rather than for it to be taken away by total strangers because the White Eagles and Arkan's men had arrived in the area as well and they said it's better to give it to us than it be given to them. And then when my husband came back in the house he gave me a full account. But in the meantime I switched the lights on and Slavoljub shouted at me, switched the lights off, and I did and then I went back in. And after five minutes my husband went back in and he told me and my father-in-law what the reason for this visit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Firstly, can you tell us roughly when this was?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: That was in early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 1992 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've mentioned Slavoljub Filipovic. Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slavoljub Filipovic, after I got married - this was several days before the war - he used to be my neighbour. But we also know each other from the secondary school. He is two years older than I am so he completed the same secondary school but just two years ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was he married to your knowledge and, if so, what was his spouse's name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was married. His wife's name is Mira Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you can help us with this, what was he like before the war in terms of his personality, as far as you knew him?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent that I knew him, he was always somebody with very strong nationalist sentiments. He was a hooligan and he was known to create disorder at school and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where did he -- you've said that he was in a neighbour, so I take it that he lived in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you were to say or if it were to be said that he lived in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Loznica, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps he was born in the village of Loznica; however, he resided in Bjelovac in my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told him -- you've told us how you saw him in uniform and with a rifle on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned this conversation about the truck and the possibility of it being taken by the TO. Did -- did Slavoljub Filipovic say to your husband what, if anything, they planned to do with the truck if they took it, Slavoljub and the other man?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They just said to him that they should take it and write down TO Fakovici or TO Skelani in order to prevent some other persons from taking the truck away. Because another Opel Kadet had been confiscated by somebody else. And in addition to that they also said that there was a lot of newly arrived person in the village, Arkan's men and White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So Slavoljub Filipovic was proposing to take this truck and to write or paint on it, I suppose, "TO Fakovici" or "TO Skelani." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On that occasion, was Slavoljub Filipovic's behaviour towards your husband appropriate in your opinion or in your perception?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because once I got to the door and I wanted to turn the light on, he -- his attitude towards me was so aggressive and improper. And my husband was very much afraid. His voice was shaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were there any other occasions in early 1992 that you saw Slavoljub Filipovic in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in early May. Jahic Mujo came to the shop where he worked and it was the shop selling agricultural equipment. Slavoljub Filipovic with another seven or eight men was there. Some of them wore camouflage uniforms and some of them wore olive-drab uniforms. They stopped Mujo from entering his shop. Slavoljub Filipovic was very insolent in his attitude and he told Mujo that Muslims were no longer allowed to work in Bjelovac and that Mujo should surrender the keys to the shop. Mujo had to obey because he saw that all of these men were wearing uniforms, so Mujo surrendered the keys and Slavoljub took over the keys from them. So Slavoljub's attitude and behaviour was awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. On this occasion was Mujo Jahic, to your knowledge, giving anything away that was socially owned?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness replied "ne," but it wasn't interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you stay in your house in the evenings, in the nights? Did you continue to spend the nights there or did there come a time when you moved and spent your nights somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remained in the house. It was daytime. A car, Jugo car, came towards -- in front of the house of Rade Ilic. It has Serbian licence plates, licence plates from Loznica. They took the children. Rade Ilic was there, his wife Rosa Ilic, and her mother Cvijeta. I came up to them and said, Why are they taking these children away from their homes? And Rade replied that he was afraid of gunfire that would scare the children. I said to him, Rade, my children are younger than your children. What's going to happen to my children? And he said to me, Take your children somewhere else, to Loznica or elsewhere. If you are afraid you can sleep in our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you take up that invitation?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I accepted the invitation. I sent the children and my father-in-law to Loznik [as interpreted], to some relatives there. And on the first night I went to sleep in Cvijeta Ilic's house. That was the agreement we had. We had agreed that I should come at around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Sorry to stop you there. Did you say that your children and father-in-law went to or did you say some other place? I think the transcript might be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. So at 10.00 you were saying you went to Cvijeta Ilic's house. Did anything happen when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As agreed, I came -- I went through the dark, I came to the front door of their house. When I opened the door I was shocked to see Slavoljub Filipovic there. I was very surprised. He was wearing a uniform and had a gun and her son Ilic, Novo, was there as well. And then also another person, Raso, who did not have a uniform. He was wearing civilian clothes. We were both surprised. They were surprised just as I was surprised. I was also scared. Cvijeta simply said -- in order to help me, said that I had come to take yeast for bread. She gave me some yeast and then escorted me out to wait for them to leave the house. She said they were on their way to stand guard somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, sorry, Raso you mentioned. Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Raso Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you return to Cvijeta's house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The two of us stood outside while they left the house. We stood there for another five minutes and then went back to the house. She took me to her bedroom to spend the night there. I was unable to sleep that whole night. At around midnight her son came, Ilic, Stojan, he only had secondary school education. And she told him, as I was listening, that I was there. He said that he didn't mind me being there and he went to sleep. That entire night I was unable to sleep at all. And towards dawn at around perhaps 4.00, Slavoljub Filipovic came back to the house, to Cvijeta's house. Her son, Novo Ilic, and he sat together in a room next to me. And I heard ammunition being dropped on to the table. I could hear the sound of that, and I could hear them counting ammunition and saying how much each of them had. I was overcome by panic. I went to the window and I stood behind the curtains and I was able to see Slobodan Djukanovic, also a neighbour of mine. He talked to somebody, but the other person was behind the corner so I couldn't see the other person. So Slobodan, Bobe, was talking and said that they had to collect young men 16 and up who did not serve the military service to Ratkovici there. These young men knew nothing about weapons and they had to undergo training there. That was the story that I heard. They were to meet someplace at around 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say the young men who had to undo -- undergo training in Ratkovici, are these young Serb men, young Muslim men, or all nationality, as far as you understand?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were Serbs, of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you leave Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a matter of clarification. My learned friend quoted at page 19, first line: "And when you say the young men who had to undergo training in Ratkovici." As I recall, she didn't mention that -- she didn't state it as such explicitly or am I mistaken in that respect? It was a kind of concluding by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see at line 24, page 18, "they had to undergo training there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I heard her saying. I have no problems with it, Mr. Wubben. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you don't need to. I mean, you have every right to ask for a clarification, but I don't think it really needs clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you leave Bjelovac at some stage and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I left it on the 11th of May, 1992, together with my husband, my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry to cut you off but we're going to take it in discrete stages with short answers, if possible. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, and where?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the village of Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were the conditions of life like in Podloznik when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: The conditions in Poloznik were awful, were terrible. Poloznik was full of refugees. In the house where I stayed there were about 80 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And these refugees were from which villages, if you can name any of them?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: People were from Zalazje, Voljevica, there were people I didn't know there, people from Bratunac fleeing towards the forest, and people somehow ended up in Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were these Muslims, Serbs, mixture?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: We were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Podloznik?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It's Poloznik. I stayed in Poloznik until the 2nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Walking. We walked for days and nights through the woods. I have no idea how we got there. The road was awful. We had no idea where we were going, but we needed to get to Srebrenica and we travelled for an entire day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, again, I won't ask you to describe the conditions of life in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies, there might be an issue with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, did you say -- just one clarification, when you walked to Srebrenica you walked for days and nights, plural, or for a day and a night?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Day and night, plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid that doesn't clarify. It's not terribly important in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Jones. I mean, let's stick to what is important, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on that theme I'm not going to ask the witness to dwell on the conditions of life in Srebrenica, in light of the indications we've received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you return to Bjelovac at any time in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime after the 20th of December of 1992 I came to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. When did you actually leave Srebrenica to go to the Bjelovac area?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I went on the 13th of December, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you went were you alone or with you with others?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were a lot of people, thousands of them, thousands of people. Because the population was stripped of everything. They were hungry. They were trying to ensure that their families stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So where did you -- where did you stay between the 13th of December and the 20th of December when you entered Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the house of my husband's uncle, Murif Sinanovic in Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you left Srebrenica in the afternoon of the 13th of December. Did you actually try to get into Bjelovac on the 14th of December or were you remaining in Poloznik?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to enter the place because I wanted to go to my house to get some food there. I had a lot of food that stayed behind in 1992. So we started out sometime at around 9.00. My neighbours and I were together in this huge crowd of people, thousands of people. So we started out in the direction of Loznicka Rijeka. And we didn't even come halfway when very strong shelling and bombing erupted. When the planes started flying over, there would usually be two of them paired together and they would fly over our heads five to six times in a day. An elderly men standing next to me died in the course of that and we started hiding under the trees, and we decided to return to Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You've mentioned strong shelling and bombing. You've described how the bombs came from these airplanes. Do you know where the shelling was coming from, from what direction?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the shells were coming from, but there were many of them, a great deal of them. And as a result of that terrible shelling, once I came to Bjelovac and my mother-in-law is buried in Bjelovac, across from the house, and once I got to Bjelovac I could see that the tombstone was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to come to that shortly. On this day, the 14th of December, 1992, you said that you couldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. Wubben. Sorry to interrupt you like this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stood up not to interrupt counsel, but he's already taking and triggering the issue itself of the day. Witness is explaining what she saw, what she experienced. And prior to that she confirmed she left Srebrenica in the afternoon of the 13th but did not indicate her experiences in time -- in a timeline. And now immediately counsel state "on this day, the 14th of December, 1992." I think that is a little bit too soon to conclude that everything is on the 14th. I think it might also be on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can address that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's about to disappear from the screen, but page 22, line 8, I think it was. The fact that she left on the 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, she left on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I asked her what she did on the 14th of December, and she said "at 9.00 a.m. we set off," so obviously she's talking about the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but let's make it -- make it clear once and for all so that we avoid further interventions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of the shelling, did you see actually where shells were falling on the 14th of December?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were falling where we were in Pirici, in Poloznik. On that day a mother who had just delivered twins two days ago was killed in Pirici. Begzadic, Nisveta, she was killed in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where did you stay that evening, the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: When I -- when we returned to Poloznik we stayed in the basement. And that night, once again I was in Poloznik staying with the relatives. And then Ibrahim Osmanovic came. He knew that I was there. He asked me to come out of the house, and I went out. Then he told me that I should go with him to another house, to Musa, whose last name I don't know, to see my neighbours, to be with them, Mira Filipovic, Dostana, her mother-in-law, and two children. And I said, Why should I go?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry to cut you off. I was going to ask you if you did subsequently go and stay in that house.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Which house do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Musa's house. Did you go to Musa's house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I went to Musa's house between 8.00 and 10.00 in the evening. In that room there were two women with three children. I was surprised and so were they. It was an unpleasant feeling. I was thinking, Why me? But when I saw those children, I was overcome by other feelings. So that evening we talked and then Musa's wife came in bringing dinner. She gave us the same food she gave her family and her children. And they refused the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to take this step by step. So you've mentioned Mira Filipovic, Dostana, her mother-in-law, and two children. First of all, do you remember what the children were? Were these Mira's children or who were the children?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Mira's and Slavoljub's children, the Filipovic children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were both children the children of Mira and Slavoljub or was one of them the children of --

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were they -- was this boys or girls or what precisely?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two children of Mira, a boy and a girl. And another 10-year-old boy called Brano.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you stay with Mira that night?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you do anything with regard to her children?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That evening I took her son Nemanja and changed diapers twice overnight and fed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did Mira say what she was doing in Bjelovac that day?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: That day, Mira didn't say anything to me. She just said that she was with the children in the attic with her mother-in-law and then Slavka Matic was throwing hand-grenades from her house and wounded her under the chest and on the head and someplace else. And that night I bandaged her wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did Mira mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Is Witness now answering a question related to happenings in Bjelovac or in the other location, the other village, Poloznik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Because she was -- excuse me. She was referring to what was happening in the evening in Poloznik, invited by counsel, and then out of a sudden there was some reference to Bjelovac. So in the time there must happened something. I don't know what. I couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think it's that difficult to follow, but I can clarify with a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did ask her what she was doing in Bjelovac that day, but go ahead, Mr. Jones, it's easier this way. Either you or she's followed the exchange so she could follow herself if you prefer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you -- Mira told you about Slavka Matic throwing hand-grenades from our house. Do you know where this was occurring?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in her house in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So in other words Mira had been in Bjelovac, had been wounded there as a result of Slavka Matic throwing hand-grenades, and then had been brought to Poloznik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's more than clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that what Mira told you?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did Mira say anything about whether she, Mira, had been in Bjelovac for the whole of 1992 or whether she had been elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: She told me that up until a fortnight ago she had been in Serbia and then he was unable to pay the rent and had to go back home to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you saw her in this house, in Musa's house, were there any Muslims in uniform in that house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were there in Musa's house or in the vicinity, did you ever see Muslims in uniforms around the house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What would you say if someone were to say that around that time there were 2.000, 2.000 Muslims in uniform with weapons going back and forth delivering messages to some sort of command centre. Did you see anything like that on that day?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, in 1992 and during the course of 1992, how many Muslims did you see in uniform, in camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how was Mira treated while she was in that house?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: There was nobody else in the house except myself and the women. And thereupon a man came along whose wife had been taken away on the 31st of May and that happened in Sikiric and she was taken away with another ten people from Sikiric and his name was Bekir Karic. He greeted them and asked whether they knew anything about the whereabouts of his wife. And Dostana replied that all she knew was that they had taken on a tractor in -- on a small tractor, in the direction of Sase and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know in fact whether the wife of Bekir Karic was ever seen again?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Bekir Karic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was she ever seen again?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you were there with Mira was she kept under an armed guard?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was she held as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a little boy who was not one of Mira's children. I think you said -- well, if you could tell us his name again, please.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Brano, Brano Vucetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How did he behave?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: He had been wounded in the face, and when I bandaged Mira's wounds he -- I tried to approach him but he was frightened. He didn't want a Muslim to go anywhere near him. And at that stage I could see that even the child who was just 10 years old was a nationalist already because he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wouldn't allow a Muslim to nurse his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he actually say that or is that an inference?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: He said, "I don't want a Muslim to bandage my wounds."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us that Mira and the others were offered food. Did they accept it?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see Mira at any time being interrogated by armed and uniformed fighters when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want you to help us with this if you can: Was it possible in 1992, I'm not just talking about December, but to travel from Poloznik to Bjelovac by car?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a narrow mountain path.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think not all of the answers -- not the witness's answer was interpreted. I think she said it was a goat path. Perhaps the witness can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Have you heard what Mr. Jones said just now? Did you say a mountain -- a goat path or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, goat path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How wide was the road from Poloznik down towards the Drina?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: The road from Poloznik to Loznicka Rijeka was the path that I was describing as a goat path. Because Poloznik is at a pretty high altitude and it is at a distance of 7 kilometres from the asphalt road going between Loznicka Rijeka and Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, for the record the witness was indicating with her arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe when you were indicating with your arms, you were indicating the width of the path?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicates a width of about 75 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if it were to be said that around this time a yellow Mercedes travelled from Poloznik to Srebrenica via Bjelovac, what would you say to that? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Poloznik area before actually going to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 20th of December, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in that period between you coming to Poloznik and then getting into Bjelovac, was there still shelling going on or had that stopped?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was incessant shelling and over that seven- to ten-day period the planes were circling over the area and there was a lot of shelling and a lot of war planes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness could be shown Exhibit D736, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for the record this is Drina Corps command strictly confidential, number 2-559, December 19, 1992. I'm obviously not going to read the whole document. I just want to draw attention to second paragraph, second sentence -- I should start from the beginning of paragraph 2. "During December 18, 19, 1992, they stabilised defence in the area of the Bratunac Brigade," and then further on: "A truck was destroyed by artillery fire as well as two motorised vehicles, aviation destroyed the department store, municipality spa Crni Guber and a part of the settlement in Srebrenica," and then this is the bit I'm going to ask you about: "And inflicted severe damages in the villages of Pirici and Poloznik as well as some personnel losses." Now, is that something you were in a position to confirm or deny that on or around 18, 19 December Serb artillery caused serious damage in the area of Pirici and Podloznik? I know it's written Poloznik, but I assume that's where you're referring to as Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She said "da." I think that's what I heard anyway. Perhaps, Madam, you could repeat your answer because the interpreter didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and thank you interpreters for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the shelling and bombing was that in the area of the goat path, as you described?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're not going to play a video, but we're going to freeze a video at certain frames. It's exhibit P428, which we've seen many times before. I'm just going to stop at about four or five places and ask the witness a few questions. So, first, we're going to stop at 0.27 and we may run up to it by a few seconds beforehand. It's the green number in the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we are at 0.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We'll play and freeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ms. Sinanovic, do you recognise where that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Jovanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think that's noted for the record that that's 0.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to stop at 2.54 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the school in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see anything burning in that frame?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're going to stop now at 4.17.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We stop there. We see smoke coming from various buildings. Do you recognise where that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Jovanovici again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we're going to 14.26.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, again, where is that, please?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Jovanovici again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then 20.44.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise where that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jovanovici, only the visibility is slightly better here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally on this, 22.24.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where is that, please?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This is in Jovanovici. This big house belonged to Miloje Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we can go now to 11.21.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- you mentioned -- well, firstly if you can tell us what you recognise in this picture.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I can recognise between the two hills -- oh, no, rather, this is Jovanovici and the road to Poloznik goes between the two hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Is Podloznik, is it on the left- or the right-hand side of those hills that we see?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: To the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that Podloznik is actually up in those hills?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then if we could stop finally at 29.36.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see a house there with smoke, what appears to be a flame. Can you take a good look at it and tell us only if you can, whose house that is.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Srecko Mihajlovic, a forest ranger from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We finished with that video and we're going to look briefly at another video which is D112. We're going to play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise the person in that video, person being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Slavoljub Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see what he was wearing in that video?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing military jacket which was a part of this olive-drab uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see him in that olive-drab uniform earlier when you described seeing him in a uniform or was he in another uniform?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning he used to wear this uniform, but when he came to my house he was wearing a camouflage uniform, when he came to take our truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. We see him saying there that his wife and two children jumped into the Drina. Is that true, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also -- well, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can give the date if that's what the issue is. On the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you myself, actually. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I recall that it was not that they jumped into the river. I recall another text as quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The text of -- the wife threw the children in the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think she jumped to Drina herself, "my mother jumped also."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She jumped to the Drina herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the point is this: To your knowledge on the 14th of December, 1992, did Mira and her two children and her mother jump or get thrown into the river Drina?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've also seen Slavoljub Filipovic saying that hundreds were killed in Bjelovac on the 14th of December, 1992. Is that true, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, the interviewer asked and Slavoljub Filipovic confirmed that jihad warriors were involved in the action in Bjelovac. To your knowledge, were jihad warriors involved in that action?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but this is the first time I've heard this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. We've finished with that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us how you had a house in Bjelovac. Do you know who, if anyone, occupies the land where your house is or was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing at the moment. I mean, the house had been destroyed, but in 1992 Slavoljub Filipovic took my house and he opened a cafe there. And afterwards he just destroyed everything, so nothing was left standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've told us that your husband is Muriz Sinanovic. Is that house the house of Muriz Sinanovic, the house you've been referring to as being taken by Slavoljub Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness can now be shown a series of photographs, it's P452. I'm trying to finish before the break, but we started slightly later. I'll probably go ten minutes into the next session, but only ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it going to be a long cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I don't expect but we still have to prepare and look into two various matters, Your Honour. We try to do as best as promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, in December 1992, I don't want to get the date wrong, but I think you said it was around the 20th or the 21st of December, 1992, did you get into the centre of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you remember the date exactly or the number -- or how many days after you first came to Poloznik? If you can give us some indication.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about when I got to Poloznik?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Bjelovac. Do you know either the approximate date when you came into Bjelovac or do you know approximately how many days it was after you left Srebrenica? That's probably a better date to fix it from.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the 20th or the 21st. I can't tell you precisely whether it was the 20th or the 21st of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a lot of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see where the shells were landing?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: They were landing everywhere, in fields, on the roads, in the streets, in the centre of Bjelovac, in Pirici, in the forest, in the villages, in Poloznik, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's something I should have asked you earlier, the Jahici, Mujici, and Lolici houses, what condition were they in in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the house in Bjelovac, the house that the Muslims had been chased away from, well some of the houses were torched and others were mined. But it was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that something which was visible in May 1992, that these houses had been torched?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: When those families left the houses, I mean the ones that were chased in the direction of Kladanj and those who were taken to the woods, the ones that were closer, they could see the houses burning. You could see it with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we look at these photographs, I actually want to start with the one which is 01088033. Now, whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my father-in-law's house, Rahmana Sinanovic's house. This is where my shop was, the ground floor of this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So if someone were to say that was the house of Vladimir Djukanovic, would that be correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No what? It would be correct or incorrect? I think you better use the word "correct" or "not correct." I repeat the question to you: "If one were to say that what you see in that photo is the house of Vladimir Djukanovic, would you say it is correct or not correct?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You have to use the words "correct" or "incorrect," Ms. Sinanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as your house in Bjelovac is concerned, was that house ever damaged? In fact, you told us it was destroyed. But before that, was it damaged by the shells or bombing or burning?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: When I got there in December 1992, either on the 20th or the 21st, I don't know, the house had been damaged by shells and aviation as well, aviation weapons. Not a lot of damage, just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you go through the rest of the photographs, we're not going to look at all of them but just a selection. I want to ask you first if you saw that house or building when you went to Bjelovac on the 20th or 21st of December, and then if you can answer at the same time whether you saw it in that condition or not. So firstly 01088029 -- in fact, first do you recognise the building?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Who does it belong to or who did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: It belonged to Ivka Ilic from Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Was there anything -- was it a private residence?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it sounded like you were going to add something. I didn't want to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say it is not Ilic Ivka, but it used to belong to Kovacevics' family where the Djokanovics had a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. So there was a cafe on that location?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a cafe run by two brothers from Kostanovici and their name was Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see that house when you went in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it in that condition?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. We're going to 8030. Firstly, do you recognise what building that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us each time what it is, please.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This is where the doctors' surgery in Bjelovac was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, did you see this building when you went in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it in this state?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Was it -- was it damaged in any way when you saw it.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just wondering --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can probably get through the photographs in another five minutes, otherwise we can break now and then just carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just the same for me. We are going to continue anyway, so let's break now. I mean, I take it you have further questions after these photos?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then we'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see Mr. Wubben standing. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to support and to try to finish today I definitely need, after my colleague finished, Mr. Jones, I need some other break to prepare further some issues left. So what I suggest is that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not -- you know that we have never said to such requests, either to you or to the Defence. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you don't need to worry about this. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My reaction is this: I've very deliberately planned my whole examination-in-chief to be finished in an hour and a half or something like that. I haven't gone into areas which I would have gone into if I had more time. It's all premised on the understanding that we finish with this witness today because that's very much her request. I understand the request of the Prosecution in the spirit of still finishing with this witness today, but simply taking a break after I finish, and obviously I don't oppose that. But I do want to have enough time to re-examine, and enough time for your questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It shouldn't be a problem. I don't know how long this cross-examination that Mr. Wubben has in mind is likely to last, but I would be surprised if it lasted a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks for your cooperation, both of you. Please proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter to clarify, Ms. Sinanovic, before we resume with the photographs, you've been referring to Poloznik. I've asked you about Podloznik. Perhaps to locate this village, could you tell us how far is it from Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 7 kilometres. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. For my purposes that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7 kilometres. From Pirici to Podloznik or Poloznik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to these photographs we were looking at 01088030 and you told us that this was what you called an ambulant or a health centre. Where in Bjelovac is this, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This was across the road from the Jahici and -- Jahic and Mujkanovic houses in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it in the centre of Bjelovac or is it outside the centre?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This is in Bjelovac but not in the centre. The area that's closer to the entry point into Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, I'm not sure if I asked you but did you see this building in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was it in the condition that we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now moving on to 01088034. And do you -- could you tell us whose house this is? Actually, there are a couple of houses, so if you could help us with each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If she prefers to look at the photo, at the exhibit itself rather than the screen, I think it would help her see better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You can also look to your right, Ms. Sinanovic, on the electronic monitor to your right. I'm going to start with the house on the left. Do you know whose house that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This house belongs to Srecko Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, you need to -- let's just be clear whether you're pointing to the left or the right and then take your time and only tell us if you're sure. Which is the house on the left and which is the house on the right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: The one on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is whose house, the one on the right?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: The one on the right is the house of Srecko Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you see that house in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did it look like it had sustained any sort of damage?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what sort of damage, if you're able to tell?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: The damage from shelling and aviation that resulted in the roof being damaged and the attic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you -- you say the house of Srecko Mihajlovic. You identified a house on the video, P428, as being in fact a burning house of Srecko Mihajlovic. Is that the same house or is it a different one? Well, let me put it this way: This Srecko Mihajlovic, did he have more than one house in the Bjelovac area?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now if we go to 8 -- 01088040, would you tell us, please, if you know whose house that is.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the house of Bozana Damjanovic. I know this house very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And did you see it in December of 1992? And if so, can you help us with any damage which you saw to the building.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this house as well. One can see that the first storey was damaged by shelling, but the ground floor is intact. It was damaged in shelling and due to aviation action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And if we go back one to 01088039, please have a look at that house. Do you know whose house that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This house is the house of Srecko Mihajlovic. The other one was not. Now that I can see it up close, I can see it better and I realise that this is the house of Srecko Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. It's no problem. Let's go back to clarify this, back to 01088034 and see now if you can tell us whose house it is. And if you don't know, feel free to say so.

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the house of Bozana Damjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So that's -- I don't think that's 01088034, which is the one that I wanted to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is 8040. That was 840.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, 01088034, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This house belongs to Milo Jovanovic, the one on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And finally can we put 01088042. Do you know whose house that is?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the house of Slavoljub Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see that house in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did it appear to have been burnt, set on fire?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see the house of Slavka Matic when you were in Bjelovac in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUHRA SINANOVIC
